items.question: A mobile games publisher runs a Claude-based refund-request triage step. The support platform aborts a triage call at 8 seconds and shows the player a generic apology. The monthly report to the executive sponsor states 'average triage latency 2.4 seconds', and the sponsor concludes performance is fine. Last month 3.1% of calls exceeded the 8-second cut-off. What should the report show instead?

options.A: The median instead of the mean, since the latency distribution is right-skewed and the median is the more robust central estimate.
options.B: The proportion of calls exceeding the 8-second cut-off, with the high percentiles reported against that threshold.
options.C: The mean with a standard deviation, so the sponsor can see the spread around the central value as well as the average itself.
options.D: Nothing different in the report; instead raise the support platform's abort timeout to 15 seconds so the 3.1% of calls complete.

items.question: A contract manufacturer codes engineering change notices with a 6-person team costing £468,000 a year fully loaded. A proposed Claude-based classifier has a one-off build cost of £190,000; annual API and platform cost of £50,400; two reviewers retained at £78,000 each; and eval-set maintenance of 0.2 FTE of an ML engineer costed at £110,000, so £22,000 a year. The sponsor's slide subtracts only the API and platform line from the baseline and reports payback in about 5.5 months. Which correction and corrected payback should the architect present?

options.A: None is needed: the retained reviewers are already inside the £468,000 baseline, so they do not reduce the saving claimed.
options.B: Net annual saving is £395,600 once eval-set maintenance is added to the platform line, giving payback of about 5.8 months.
options.C: Net annual saving is £261,600 once the two retained reviewers' salaries are counted, giving payback of about 8.7 months.
options.D: Net annual saving is £239,600 with retained reviewers and eval maintenance counted, giving payback of about 9.5 months.

items.question: Why does an architecture decision record document the options that were rejected, and not only the option chosen?

options.A: Because governance frameworks require at least three options to be documented for every architecture decision.
options.B: Because rejected options become the enhancement backlog once the chosen option has been delivered.
options.C: So a later reader can see what was already evaluated, why it lost, and whether the reason still holds.
options.D: Because the rejected options serve as the rollback plan if the chosen option fails in production.

items.question: Six weeks ago an architect told a retail bank's steering committee that its Claude-based mortgage document checker 'will not miss a missing payslip — we've tested it'. A production audit of 1,200 cases has now found 14 misses, 3 of which reached an underwriter decision. On the strength of the original statement, the operations director instructed branch staff to stop double-checking the payslip field. The next committee is in nine days. What is the best next step?

options.A: Raise it at the next committee in nine days with the audit results and a corrective plan, so the correction reaches the committee with a solution attached.
options.B: Reinstate the branch double-check with the operations director today, then send the committee a written correction before the meeting giving the measured miss rate.
options.C: Amend the earlier minute to record the statement as 'a very low miss rate is expected', then brief the committee verbally when it next meets.
options.D: Commission a larger audit first, so the miss rate can be reported with a defensible confidence interval rather than from 1,200 cases alone.

items.question: In an SLO agreement covering a Claude-based service, what is an error budget?

options.A: A financial provision set aside to pay service credits to users when the service misbehaves.
options.B: The maximum number of retries a client may issue with backoff before a request is abandoned.
options.C: The quantity of failure the target permits over the window, consumed as failures occur and used to govern releases.
options.D: The proportion of the offline evaluation set the team has agreed to treat as permanently unfixable failures.

items.question: A water utility's architecture board has approved an eight-page ADR choosing an orchestrator–workers design over a single agent for permit-application processing, on the grounds of trajectory auditability, failure containment between steps, and a stated increase in cost per application. The CIO has three minutes at the executive committee. What framing should the architect supply?

options.A: The pattern names and the measured token overhead per application of each design, since the committee funds the technology and should understand what it is buying.
options.B: The cost-per-application increase on its own, quoted as an annual figure, since cost is the only dimension an executive committee can meaningfully act on.
options.C: A note that the orchestrator–workers choice is technical and internal to the architecture board, so no executive committee time is required.
options.D: Regulator-reconstructable permit decisions and failures contained to one step, at the stated increase per application, with the full ADR linked.

items.question: An insurer's procurement director mandates a second model vendor 'so we are not dependent on one supplier' for a Claude-based claims-summary service handling 9,000 claims a day. The team's prompt library, guardrails, output validators and 1,400-case eval suite are all tuned to the incumbent. What should the architect propose?

options.A: Run both vendors active-active with claims traffic split between them, so failover is continuously proven in production rather than rehearsed.
options.B: Sign a standby contract with the second vendor to satisfy the mandate, but route no live claims traffic to it until a switch is actually needed.
options.C: Address concentration risk through portability: an abstraction boundary, versioned prompt and eval assets, and a rehearsed migration with the switch time recorded.
options.D: Decline the mandate on the grounds that prompts, guardrails and output validators tuned to one model do not transfer, making a second vendor technically unachievable.

items.question: A local authority children's-services department has deployed input and output guardrails around a Claude-based case-note summarisation tool. The information governance board asks the architect for a written residual risk statement. Which TWO elements make the statement usable by the board rather than merely reassuring? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: An assurance from the architect that the guardrails reduce the risk to a level the department can accept.
options.B: The measured rate at which guardrails failed to block a known adversarial test set, with its date and size.
options.C: A statement that residual risk falls to zero once both the input and output guardrail layers are enabled.
options.D: The detection and response path when a failure gets through: who is alerted, by what signal, and the time to containment.
options.E: The model provider's published safety documentation and system card for the underlying model.

items.question: A university's student-services team demonstrated a Claude-based enquiry assistant using twelve hand-picked questions. Every answer was excellent and the pro-vice-chancellor now expects that quality across all enquiries. What correction matters most before the pilot is scoped?

options.A: Extend the demonstration to fifty hand-picked questions drawn from the same enquiry categories, so confidence rests on a broader base before the pilot is scoped.
options.B: Say the twelve questions were hand-picked, and re-set expectations against a random sample of real enquiry traffic, malformed and out-of-scope included.
options.C: Explain that demonstration quality is unrepresentative because demos run without production latency, rate limiting and concurrent load.
options.D: Add an interface disclaimer telling students that answers may be incorrect and should be checked with a member of student-services staff.

items.question: A port operator is asked by a shipping-line customer to sign a 99.95% monthly availability SLA for a Claude-based container-documentation checker. Each check calls, in series, the operator's gateway, the model provider, and a national customs reference API whose owner publishes 99.5% availability and offers no better tier. What should the architect say?

options.A: Sign the 99.95% target and add aggressive retry with exponential backoff against the customs API, since retries recover the large majority of transient failures.
options.B: Sign the 99.95% target but exclude from measurement every minute in which the national customs API is unavailable, so the figure reflects only what the port operator itself controls.
options.C: Offer 99.95% on the model call in isolation, which is the component the SLA is really about, and leave the gateway and customs integration out of scope.
options.D: A serial chain cannot exceed its weakest link, so 99.5% caps the achievable figure: renegotiate the target, or serve customs data from a cache with a stated staleness bound.

items.question: How do an SLI, an SLO and an SLA differ?

options.A: An SLI is the internal target, an SLO is the customer-facing promise, and an SLA is the schedule of penalties attached to that promise.
options.B: An SLI covers latency, an SLO covers availability, and an SLA covers output quality such as summary faithfulness.
options.C: An SLI is the measurement, an SLO the target set on it, and an SLA the external commitment with consequences attached.
options.D: An SLI and an SLO are interchangeable terms; an SLA adds a requirement that the metric be monitored continuously in production.

items.question: An energy retailer deployed a Claude-based billing-complaint responder in the same month it retrained its complaint-handling team and changed its refund authorisation policy. Average handling time fell 31% over the following quarter, and the programme lead's board paper attributes the whole fall to the assistant. How should the benefit be presented?

options.A: As a 31% combined effect of three simultaneous changes, the assistant's share unattributed, plus a design to isolate it — a held-out team or a staggered regional rollout.
options.B: Attributed across the three changes in proportion to their implementation cost, the only objective split available in the programme's own financials.
options.C: Attributed in full to the assistant, since it is the only one of the three changes with a direct mechanism for reducing handling time per contact.
options.D: Deferred for a full year of data, by which point the effects of the retraining and the policy change will have washed out and the residual improvement can be credited to the assistant.

items.question: A mining company's safety function uses Claude to extract hazard observations from free-text shift reports. The HSE director asks for a numeric confidence score on every extraction so supervisors can review anything below 80%. The team can have the model emit a self-assessed confidence field in its structured output within a day, and 900 extractions have already been manually adjudicated. What is the best next step?

options.A: Emit the self-assessed confidence field and set the review threshold at 80% as requested, monitoring supervisor override rates over the first month.
options.B: Decline the request and explain that language models cannot produce numeric confidence estimates of any kind for their own extractions.
options.C: Test candidate signals against the 900 adjudicated extractions, then set the threshold from the measured separation and supervisor review capacity.
options.D: Replace the score with a fixed random 20% review sample of all extractions, which removes the need for any confidence signal.

items.question: A public transport authority's CTO proposes replacing the hosted Claude service behind its accessibility-request triage with a self-hosted open-weights model, arguing it 'removes the per-token bill'. Which TWO cost categories must be added on the self-hosted side for the comparison to be honest? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: Reserved accelerator capacity sized for peak concurrency, paid through every quiet period whether or not requests arrive.
options.B: Maintenance and re-labelling of the triage evaluation set as the authority's accessibility policies change from year to year.
options.C: Engineering capacity to run serving infrastructure — upgrades, scaling and on-call — that the hosted service absorbs today.
options.D: Human review of triage decisions, which the authority's policy requires before an accessibility request is actioned.
options.E: Per-token inference charges levied on every triage request served by the self-hosted model, billed on the same meter as today.

items.question: A hotel group's revenue team presents a twelve-month cost forecast for a Claude-based rate-plan explanation service. A large shared policy preamble is sent on every request, and the forecast applies the reduced cached-input cost to 100% of requests. Booking traffic clusters into two daily peaks with long quiet periods overnight and mid-afternoon. What is the correct fix to the forecast?

options.A: Remove the caching assumption entirely and forecast at full input cost throughout the year, as the conservative position.
options.B: Enlarge the shared policy preamble so a greater share of every request is cacheable, improving the ratio of cached to uncached input tokens.
options.C: Keep the 100% cached assumption and add a contingency percentage to the annual total to cover the uncertainty.
options.D: Model an explicit cache-hit rate from the observed arrival pattern and present the saving as a range with the uncached case as the floor.

items.question: A medical device manufacturer's regulatory affairs team requires an ADR covering the decision to pin the Claude model version behind its post-market surveillance complaint classifier. Which THREE items must the ADR state so that a reviewer a year from now can judge whether the decision is still valid? (Choose THREE.)

options.A: Why pinning was chosen over tracking the latest version: any behaviour change triggers re-validation under the quality management system.
options.B: The exact token counts of the classifier prompt and its few-shot examples, as measured on the decision date against the pinned model version.
options.C: The conditions that require the pin to be revisited, such as a provider deprecation notice or a validated challenger improvement.
options.D: The name of the engineer who set the version string in the deployment manifest, the date applied, and the change ticket reference.
options.E: The recurring cost the pin imposes: re-validation owed each time it moves, and the risk of one large migration instead of several small ones.

items.question: A stakeholder asks what accuracy to expect from a Claude-based system the team has not yet built. Which form of answer is most defensible?

options.A: A single figure taken from the closest published benchmark for a task of this kind, cited as the expected accuracy.
options.B: A range with its basis stated — comparable systems the team has measured — and the factors that would move it to each end.
options.C: A refusal to estimate, on the grounds that nothing can be said until the system exists and has been measured.
options.D: The accuracy target the stakeholder has already stated, since that is the requirement the build will be held to anyway.

items.question: A courier network's largest customer has signed an agreement containing a service credit payable 'whenever a delivery-exception explanation produced by the system is inaccurate'. The clause defines no measurement method, no sample, and no adjudicator. What is the specific defect the architect should raise with legal?

options.A: A financial obligation turns on a per-incident judgement the agreement never defines; a workable clause names the sample, the rubric, the grader and the threshold.
options.B: The service credit is too small to alter the supplier's behaviour, so the clause creates an obligation without any real incentive to improve.
options.C: Probabilistic systems should not carry output-quality service credits at all, because any such commitment will eventually be breached at scale.
options.D: The term 'inaccurate' should be replaced with 'hallucinated', which has an established technical definition in the research literature and is measurable.

items.question: In a steering committee paper, what distinguishes a decision item from an information item?

options.A: A decision item includes the supporting analysis in full; an information item is a one-paragraph summary of delivery progress.
options.B: A decision item is tabled by the programme sponsor; an information item is tabled by the delivery team lead.
options.C: A decision item concerns budget or scope; an information item concerns delivery progress and milestones.
options.D: A decision item names the choice, the options and a recommendation; an information item reports status and asks nothing.

items.question: A property portal's commercial director wants the public product page for a Claude-based listing-description generator to state that the system 'never invents facts about a property'. Descriptions are generated from structured listing fields plus the agent's free-text notes, and a post-generation validator checks each factual assertion back against the source fields. What should the architect propose the page say?

options.A: Retain 'never invents facts' and add small-print advising that generated descriptions should be verified by the listing agent before they are published.
options.B: Say the system 'uses advanced AI to ensure accuracy', which conveys the benefit to buyers without committing to a specific measurable claim.
options.C: Describe the mechanism: facts drawn from named listing fields, unmatched assertions removed not published, with the validator's measured catch rate.
options.D: Make no factuality claim on the product page and address the topic in the terms of service instead, where the general disclaimer already sits.

items.question: A film studio's post-production group must choose between two designs for a Claude-based dialogue-continuity checker. Option 1 has been prototyped and measured on 500 scenes. Option 2 exists only as a design. The proposed slide puts both into one table with accuracy, latency and cost-per-episode columns, all shown as single figures. Which TWO changes make the comparison honest? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: Drop Option 2 from the table until it has been prototyped and measured to the same standard as Option 1 was.
options.B: Mark each cell with its provenance — measured on 500 scenes, vendor-supplied, or engineering estimate — so rows can be weighted.
options.C: Show the unbuilt option's cells as ranges with the assumption driving each, not point values identical in form to measured ones.
options.D: Collapse the three columns into a single weighted score so the two options can be ranked without the reader having to interpret them.
options.E: Show only the accuracy column, since latency and cost per episode cannot be known for an option that has not been built.

items.question: Seven weeks into the quarter, a vehicle manufacturer's aftersales platform team finds its Claude-based warranty-claim assessor is running at 2.4 times forecast cost. The cause is dealers pasting whole service-history PDFs into a free-text field, inflating input tokens. At the current rate the quarterly budget is exhausted in about three weeks. Capping input size would make the assessor reject or truncate the pasted histories dealers currently rely on. The budget owner is the aftersales director, who has not yet been told. What is the best next step?

options.A: Apply the input cap and a summarisation pre-step immediately, then report the overrun to the director once the run rate is back within forecast.
options.B: Tell the aftersales director now, with the measured run rate, the cause, the exhaustion date, and both options: fund the overrun, or cap what dealers can submit.
options.C: Request a budget increase from the aftersales director framed as unanticipated adoption success, and take the technical analysis to the quarterly review.
options.D: Impose a hard per-dealer request quota so spend cannot exceed the quarterly budget, and raise the matter at the next quarterly review.

items.question: A new owning team asks why a guardrail was placed before retrieval rather than after. Which artefact is supposed to answer that question?

options.A: The service runbook used by the on-call operations team.
options.B: The architecture decision record for guardrail placement.
options.C: The system design document describing the request path.
options.D: The production readiness review record signed before launch.

items.question: A retail pharmacy chain piloted a Claude-based prescription-query assistant on 2,000 queries from one region and measured £0.031 per query. The finance case multiplies that by a forecast 4.1 million annual queries to reach £127,100. In the two regions excluded from the pilot, queries routinely arrive with scanned prescription images attached and substantially longer patient histories. What correction should the architect make?

options.A: Apply a 20% contingency to the £127,100 to absorb cost variation between the piloted and the excluded regions.
options.B: Re-base the forecast on the highest per-query cost observed anywhere in the pilot region, giving a deliberately conservative worst case for the committee.
options.C: Re-measure on a sample stratified by region and input type, scanned images and long histories included, and give the annual figure as a range.
options.D: Keep the £127,100 and add a monthly true-up against actual invoices so the budget self-corrects once real usage is known.

items.question: A staffing firm's Claude-based CV-to-role matching assistant is under board review before scale-up. The commercial director reports accuracy of 0.62, defined as the share of shortlists a recruiter accepts with no edits. The data science lead reports 0.94, defined as the share of individual candidate-role matches an adjudicator judges correct. A typical shortlist contains eight matches. Both figures are measured correctly. What should the architect put in front of the board?

options.A: Both figures with their units: a per-match rate of 0.94 across eight matches gives roughly 0.61 for a clean shortlist, consistent with the observed 0.62.
options.B: The adjudicated per-match figure of 0.94 as the official metric, since it is independently adjudicated and less exposed to individual recruiter preference.
options.C: A single blended accuracy figure averaging the per-match and per-shortlist measurements, so the board is not shown contradictory numbers.
options.D: The commercial figure of 0.62 alone, since only recruiter acceptance of a whole shortlist reflects whether the system is actually useful.

items.question: An aircraft-maintenance provider uses Claude to draft work cards. One draft omitted a torque value from a task step. A technician caught it during the mandatory second-person check; no aircraft was affected. The provider's AI incident policy requires reporting only events with customer or safety impact, and the AI governance forum meets monthly. What should the architect do?

options.A: Record it in the team's defect tracker; no report to the forum is required, since impact was zero and the policy reporting threshold was not met.
options.B: Report it to the forum as a safety-impact incident, since an omitted torque value on a work card is a safety-critical defect by nature.
options.C: Hold it until a second occurrence, so the forum's monthly slot is spent on established patterns rather than isolated one-off events.
options.D: Report it as a near miss, with the mechanism behind the omission, the control that caught it, and whether that control covers every draft path.

items.question: In a risk register entry for an AI system, why is detectability recorded alongside likelihood and impact?

options.A: Because two risks of equal likelihood and impact need different controls if one is visible and the other is silent.
options.B: Because regulators require a three-factor score on every AI-related entry in the risk register.
options.C: Because detectability determines which team is assigned ownership of the risk and its controls.
options.D: Because a third dimension gives the register more sorting and filtering options for board reporting.

items.question: A specialty insurer's model risk function asks the architect to cost a migration of its Claude-based underwriting-referral summariser from its currently pinned version to a successor, so the amount can be provisioned annually. Which TWO items are the substantial recurring costs of that migration for this system? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: Renegotiating the commercial agreement and rate card the insurer holds with the model provider.
options.B: Re-running the eval suite and adjudicating every case where the successor disagrees with the pinned version.
options.C: Rebuilding the retrieval index, since embeddings must be regenerated whenever the generation model changes.
options.D: Rewriting the application code that issues the model call and parses the returned response.
options.E: Re-tuning the prompt and guardrails fitted to the pinned version, and re-obtaining model risk sign-off.

items.question: A waste management company's business case for a Claude-based route-exception triage system shows a three-year net benefit of £1.4m across fourteen assumptions. Sensitivity analysis shows that varying one of them — the automation rate, the share of exceptions closed without a dispatcher — between 45% and 75% swings the three-year net from −£0.2m to £2.6m. Every other assumption moves the result by less than £0.15m. The three-week pilot measured 58%. How should the case go to the investment committee?

options.A: As the £1.4m three-year point estimate, with all fourteen assumptions documented in an appendix for any member who wishes to interrogate them.
options.B: Led by the automation rate: the pilot's 58% on a three-week basis, the break-even rate of roughly 47%, and a stage gate releasing the next tranche once confirmed.
options.C: As a Monte Carlo distribution over all fourteen assumptions, giving the committee a probability distribution over the three-year net rather than a single point figure.
options.D: Withheld until the pilot has run long enough for the automation rate to stabilise, since presenting a case that turns on an unstable input is premature.

items.question: A construction group's commercial manager reports that the Claude-based subcontractor-claim summariser 'gave a different answer this morning to the one it gave yesterday for the same claim', and nothing in the claim pack was edited. Which TWO statements belong in the architect's reply? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: Wording can differ between calls on identical input through sampling variation; what is guaranteed is that every figure traces to a named field in the pack, verified on both runs.
options.B: Differences of this kind are eliminated entirely by setting temperature to zero, so this indicates a configuration error the team will correct in today's release.
options.C: The difference shows the model itself has changed underneath the service and that the version pin in the deployment manifest has failed.
options.D: The retrieved context may also have differed if the pack was re-indexed overnight; that is a separate, checkable cause, and the request log records what was supplied.
options.E: Language models return different output on every call, so no consistency of any kind can be expected from the summariser or the figures it quotes.

items.question: An online travel agency streams a Claude-generated itinerary-change explanation to the customer's browser while a downstream job waits for the finished text to update the booking record. Product proposes an SLO of 'response within 2 seconds'. Engineering notes that first tokens appear in under a second but full streaming takes six to nine seconds. What should the SLO specify?

options.A: The 2-second target measured to completion, with generated output length reduced until streaming finishes inside the target.
options.B: The 2-second target measured to first token, treating the completion measure as an internal engineering concern only.
options.C: Two objectives: time to first token for the customer, and time to completion for the booking update, each with its own target.
options.D: A single objective on the mean of the first-token and completion times, so one number covers both ends of the streamed response.

items.question: A rail infrastructure operator's programme board asks whether a Claude-based track-inspection-report triage system will meet a 0.95 recall target on safety-critical defects. The team has 260 labelled reports and has not yet measured anything. The honest answer is that they do not know. Which THREE elements must that answer contain to be useful to the board? (Choose THREE.)

options.A: The measurement that would settle it, and the sample size needed to separate 0.95 from 0.90 with confidence.
options.B: The date by which that measurement will exist, and the labelling support the team needs to hit it.
options.C: The team's current belief expressed as a recall range, with the basis on which that range rests.
options.D: A commitment to the 0.95 recall figure, conditional on the board funding the next phase of delivery.
options.E: An assurance that recall on safety-critical defects is already the team's highest engineering priority.

items.question: A semiconductor manufacturer classifies wafer-defect reports with a prompt carrying 240 curated few-shot examples. Input cost per request is dominated by those examples, p95 latency sits above the fab's inline budget, and quality on the 1,500-case eval is already acceptable. The team proposes fine-tuning to move the examples into the weights. How should the architect frame the recommendation to the steering group?

options.A: As inadvisable: pruning and compacting the curated example set should be attempted first and will always recover the latency without a training step.
options.B: As premature: fine-tuning exists to raise quality on the eval, so it is warranted only once measured quality is unacceptable.
options.C: As a permanent removal of the prompt-engineering cost, since the behaviour lives in the weights and the examples no longer have to be maintained.
options.D: As behavioural compression rather than new knowledge, conditional on a stable task definition, the 1,500-case eval remaining the gate, and re-tuning costed in.

items.question: Why is cost per resolved case a better executive metric for a Claude-based support deflection system than cost per API call?

options.A: Because it absorbs the cost of conversations that escalate, so it cannot be improved by shedding hard cases.
options.B: Because it produces a smaller headline number and is therefore easier to get through budget approval.
options.C: Because per-call costs move with the provider's published pricing, which is outside the team's control.
options.D: Because executives are unfamiliar with token-based units and prefer metrics denominated in cases.

items.question: A national benefits agency wants an internal quality objective on its Claude-based eligibility-evidence summariser: 'summaries must be materially accurate'. The service produces 22,000 summaries a week, and a trained assessor takes about 12 minutes to adjudicate one. The agency has funded a single assessor, who has roughly 37 working hours a week. What structure makes the objective operable?

options.A: Adjudicate only the summaries the model itself flags with low confidence, concentrating the single assessor's time where errors are most likely.
options.B: Define material accuracy in a rubric, sample about 185 summaries a week at random, and report the rate with an interval plus the action if it falls below target.
options.C: Require assessor sign-off on every summary before it is issued to a caseworker, since full per-item certification is the only structure that guarantees the objective.
options.D: State the objective qualitatively and treat caseworker complaints about summaries as the signal that quality has fallen below it.

items.question: A crop-science company's CEO argues that thirty years of proprietary field-trial data is the firm's competitive advantage, and that the advantage is only captured by fine-tuning it into a model rather than 'handing it to a retrieval system anyone could build'. The current service answers agronomists' questions by retrieving from the trial database with citations to individual trials; agronomists say that per-trial traceability is why they trust it. What is the strongest response?

options.A: Agree in principle and propose fine-tuning on the thirty-year trial corpus while keeping a retrieval layer alongside it purely to supply the citations.
options.B: Argue that thirty years of field-trial records is too small a corpus for fine-tuning to produce a measurable effect on answers.
options.C: The moat is exclusive access to the data either way, while fine-tuning dissolves the trials into weights and removes the citation agronomists rely on.
options.D: Argue that fine-tuning would expose the proprietary trial corpus to the model provider in a way that retrieval from the firm's own database does not.

items.question: A managed-services provider is agreeing availability terms for a Claude-based ticket-triage service sold to enterprise clients. The design falls back to a smaller model tier when the primary is unavailable, and to a rules-based router when both are. Which TWO points must the agreement settle for the stated availability figure to mean anything to the client? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: The provider's internal alert thresholds and timers for switching automatically between the three tiers.
options.B: Which of the two fallback tiers is entered first when the primary model tier becomes unavailable.
options.C: Whether time served by each fallback tier counts as available, degraded, or unavailable for the purposes of the figure.
options.D: The quality floor that must hold while a fallback is serving, since counting that time as available asserts fitness for purpose.
options.E: The specific model versions used in each serving tier, so the client can verify the provider's stated capability claims.

items.question: At what granularity should architecture decision records be written?

options.A: One per service, revised in place as the service evolves and is extended.
options.B: One per sprint, summarising all the decisions taken during that sprint.
options.C: One per release, so the record set aligns with what was actually deployed.
options.D: One per significant, hard-to-reverse decision, written when the decision is made.

items.question: A rail freight operator's sponsor wants the architect to commit at next week's programme board to a go-live date for a Claude-based wagon-defect report triage system. The system has no eval set, no measured accuracy and no agreed acceptance threshold. The build is roughly two-thirds complete and the team estimates four more weeks of engineering. What should the architect commit to at the board?

options.A: The four-week engineering estimate plus a two-week contingency buffer, given to the board as the go-live date.
options.B: A date for the measurement and acceptance decision, with a proposed threshold and an eval-set plan, so the board can call go or no-go then.
options.C: No date at all until an eval set exists and accuracy has been measured against it, since any date offered before then would simply be invented.
options.D: Go-live conditional on the system exceeding 0.9 accuracy on the defect-triage task, which gives the board both a date and a quality bar.

items.question: A broadband provider's care organisation runs a Claude-based first-line assistant across 600,000 conversations a month at £0.09 of inference per conversation. 38% of conversations escalate to a human agent, and an agent-handled contact costs £4.10. Before the assistant, all 600,000 contacts were agent-handled. Which figure should the team put in front of the operations director as the unit economics?

options.A: £1.65 per contact handled end to end — inference on all 600,000 plus agent cost on the 228,000 escalated — against £4.10 before.
options.B: £0.09 per conversation, since that is the marginal cost the assistant adds and agent cost sits in the care organisation's own budget.
options.C: £0.15 per resolved contact — total inference divided by the 372,000 contacts resolved without an agent — since only those represent the assistant's output.
options.D: £1.61 per contact, excluding inference spent on conversations that went on to escalate, since that spend produced no resolution.

items.question: What must the Context section of an architecture decision record capture?

options.A: The forces in effect at the time — constraints, deadlines, team capacity — including those too obvious to write down.
options.B: A description of the system architecture as it stood immediately before the decision, component by component.
options.C: The business justification for the programme the decision sits within, as set out in the funding case.
options.D: The stakeholders consulted before the choice, and the position each of them took on the options.

items.question: In an AI business case, what distinguishes a hard benefit from a soft benefit?

options.A: A hard benefit can be measured objectively; a soft benefit is inherently unmeasurable and can only be asserted in the case.
options.B: A hard benefit removes a cost from a budget line; a soft benefit improves something real that no budget line records.
options.C: A hard benefit is realised inside the first year of operation; a soft benefit accrues over a longer horizon.
options.D: A hard benefit is guaranteed by a contract or a signed commitment; a soft benefit is an estimate.

items.question: Why is an internal SLO normally set tighter than the SLA it backs?

options.A: Because internal teams need a stretch target above the contractual figure to maintain performance discipline.
options.B: Because SLAs are measured over longer windows than SLOs, so the tighter internal figure compensates for that averaging.
options.C: Because external auditors require two distinct thresholds for every externally committed service.
options.D: Because the gap is a warning margin: crossing the internal target pulls attention while the commitment is intact.

items.question: A team describes its architect as well calibrated. Assessed over a long series of statements, what does that mean?

options.A: The architect's estimates usually land close to the outcome that eventually occurs.
options.B: Among the statements made with 80% confidence, close to 80% turned out to be true.
options.C: The architect never states a confidence level without documented evidence to support it.
options.D: The architect's estimates are deliberately conservative, so actual outcomes usually beat them.

items.question: Why does fine-tuning fail to keep a system's answers factually current?

options.A: Because knowledge in weights is fixed at training time and changes only on retraining, while the facts keep moving.
options.B: Because fine-tuned models lose the ability to follow instructions about preferring recent information.
options.C: Because fine-tuning datasets cannot contain dated material such as effective-from timestamps.
options.D: Because a fine-tuned model cannot be combined with a retrieval layer that supplies it with current facts at request time.

items.question: In a Claude-based system with a mandatory human review step, which cost fails to amortise as processed volume grows?

options.A: The build cost of the integration with the surrounding operational systems.
options.B: The cost of maintaining and re-labelling the evaluation set as the task changes.
options.C: The cost of developing, reviewing and versioning the prompt library.
options.D: Human review, incurred per item and therefore rising in step with volume.

items.question: What makes a head-to-head comparison of two models decision-grade for a production system?

options.A: Both are evaluated on the same public benchmark under identical settings, with the same scoring script applied to each.
options.B: Both run on the same task-specific eval set with comparable tuning effort, and latency, output format and safety measured on both.
options.C: Both are given the incumbent's tuned production prompt unchanged, so neither candidate receives special treatment.
options.D: The challenger is evaluated on the cases where the incumbent currently fails, since that is where any improvement would have to show up.

items.question: Why should an architecture decision record be written when the decision is taken rather than reconstructed afterwards?

options.A: Because the information and constraints present when choosing are the record's substance and cannot be recovered later.
options.B: Because the organisation's governance framework requires design documentation to exist before implementation begins.
options.C: Because reconstructing the record later takes considerably more effort than writing it at the time.
options.D: Because the decision cannot be implemented until the record has been reviewed and approved.

items.question: Why is 'time to a human decision when the system defers' often a better contractual commitment than an output accuracy figure?

options.A: Because it is cheaper for the supplier to guarantee than any output accuracy figure would be.
options.B: Because accuracy is a property of the model and therefore the model provider's responsibility rather than the integrator's.
options.C: Because it is measurable from timestamps and bounds the customer's worst case however the model performs on an item.
options.D: Because customers in practice care more about speed of resolution than about the correctness of the answer.

items.question: A payments company had four days to choose between two integration approaches for its Claude-based dispute-narrative service before a card scheme deadline, and chose on partial evidence. Two weeks later the architect is writing the ADR. Which THREE things must the record state? (Choose THREE.)

options.A: That the choice was made against a four-day scheme deadline, and which evidence was consequently not gathered.
options.B: The evidence that would have been gathered with more time, and whether gathering it now would still change anything.
options.C: The outcome over the two weeks since go-live, presented as confirmation that the choice was sound.
options.D: The revisit trigger — what observation would cause the team to reopen the choice now the deadline has passed.
options.E: An acknowledgement of the process shortfall and a commitment to allow adequate time on future decisions of this kind.

items.question: A media monitoring company routed 70% of its Claude-based article-tagging traffic from the higher capability tier to a cheaper one and reports a 44% reduction in monthly inference spend to its executive team. Which TWO things must accompany that figure for it to be a decision-grade claim? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: A commitment that no traffic will be routed back to the higher tier, so the saving is durable across quarters and can be booked in the budget.
options.B: The measured quality delta on the eval set for the traffic that moved, so the saving can be weighed against its quality cost.
options.C: The share of the company's overall cloud and data-platform spend that inference now represents after the reroute.
options.D: The definition of the routing rule that selects the 70%, since the saving holds only while the traffic mix resembles the calibration set.
options.E: An assurance from the provider that the cheaper tier will remain available for the life of the service contract.

items.question: A clinical-documentation vendor's sales lead wants to quote '94% accuracy' for its Claude-based discharge-letter summariser in a hospital tender response. Which TWO conditions must hold before that figure goes into the document? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: The figure travels with the population measured, the sample size, the date, and the model and prompt versions in effect.
options.B: The response states that the figure is indicative only, which removes any need to describe how it was produced.
options.C: The figure has been independently reproduced by a third-party clinical auditor and certified before the response is submitted.
options.D: The same figure has already been achieved on the tendering hospital's own document mix and case load, measured before submission.
options.E: The grading rubric is stated, since accuracy for a clinical letter summary is a rubric judgement, not an objective match.

items.question: In a supervisory meeting, a financial regulator asks the architect what the accuracy of the firm's Claude-based suitability-assessment summariser is. The most recent measurement, 0.91, comes from an eval run eleven months ago, against a model version that has since changed twice and a prompt that has been revised three times. The architect must answer in the room. What should the answer be?

options.A: Give 0.91 as the firm's accuracy figure, noting that it is the most recent measurement the eval programme has produced.
options.B: Give 0.91, note that it predates two model changes and three prompt revisions and so does not describe today's system, and commit to a remeasurement date.
options.C: Decline to give any figure in the room, on the basis that quoting a stale number to a regulator is worse than saying nothing.
options.D: Give 0.91 and add that the model changes and prompt revisions since were improvements, so current accuracy is at least that.

items.question: A pet insurer's marketing team wants the launch page for its Claude-based claims assistant to read 'instant decisions on every claim'. In production, 22% of claims are deferred to a human assessor with a stated two-working-day turnaround, and a further 4% are stopped by a guardrail and re-routed. Launch is in six days. What is the best next step?

options.A: Approve the copy: 74% of claims do receive an instant decision, and launch copy is understood to describe the intended experience rather than a guarantee.
options.B: Ask marketing to drop every reference to decision speed and describe the assistant's capabilities in general terms instead of numbers.
options.C: Escalate the wording to the legal team for a view on whether it is misleading, and let them determine the final launch copy.
options.D: Give marketing accurate wording backed by the figures: instant decisions on around three quarters of claims, the rest assessed within two working days.

items.question: A digital bank's platform team plans to tell the CFO that 'unit cost per thousand tokens fell 31% after the optimisation programme'. Over the same six months, monthly inference spend rose from £84,000 to £119,000, and monthly requests rose from 6.1 million to 12.6 million. What should the report say?

options.A: Cost per request fell from £0.0138 to £0.0094 while volume more than doubled, so total monthly spend rose 42% to £119,000.
options.B: The 31% unit improvement alone, since total spend is a function of demand and demand is set by product, not by the platform team.
options.C: The increase in total spend alone, since that is the figure the CFO's budget carries and unit improvements are an internal engineering matter.
options.D: The 31% unit improvement together with the spend the bank would have incurred at the old unit cost, presenting the difference as a saving delivered.

items.question: A regional health board must retain, for six years, the full prompt, retrieved context and response for every call to its Claude-based referral-letter triage service, to satisfy its clinical records policy. Volume is 30,000 calls a month. Which TWO cost lines does this requirement add that a business case scoped on inference spend would miss? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: The per-call token cost of the retrieved context that is sent to the model at request time on every triage call.
options.B: The model provider's own logging of these requests, retained on the provider's side under its own policy.
options.C: Storage compounding across six years, since retained context dwarfs the responses and the archive never shrinks.
options.D: Re-embedding the retained records periodically so the six-year archive stays semantically searchable as the embedding model changes.
options.E: Building and operating an access-controlled, tamper-evident path so a specific record can be produced on request.

items.question: A Nordic public-sector shared-services organisation runs a Claude-based citizen-correspondence classifier under a published commitment that all processing of citizen data takes place within a named region. A new supplier offers a materially cheaper model, served only from a region outside that commitment. The finance director asks why the team is not switching. What is the strongest response?

options.A: That the cheaper model would classify citizen correspondence less accurately, so the saving would be offset by classification rework.
options.B: That the published processing-location commitment is a feasibility filter, not a cost trade-off: a supplier that cannot meet it is not in the comparison set.
options.C: That the organisation could route only the correspondence containing no personal data to the cheaper supplier outside the region, capturing part of the saving.
options.D: That the payloads could be encrypted before leaving the region, so the published commitment is satisfied while the cheaper supplier is used.

items.question: A freight forwarder's Claude-based customs-classification agent completes each case in five tool-using steps: extract the goods description, retrieve tariff candidates, apply exclusion rules, check origin documentation, and issue the classification with justification. Final classifications are correct 88% of the time. The sponsor wants that one figure in a board pack that is asking the board to approve a remediation budget. What should the architect provide?

options.A: The 88% figure alone, since the board is accountable for outcomes rather than for the internals of the agent pipeline.
options.B: The product of the five per-step success rates, which gives the true end-to-end accuracy the 88% headline overstates.
options.C: The per-step success rates only, since the remediation budget will be spent on individual steps rather than on the pipeline taken as a whole.
options.D: The 88% figure with the distribution of failures across the five steps, since two systems at 88% with failures in different steps need different remediation.

items.question: A health insurer ran a ten-week pilot of a Claude-based claims-triage assistant with twelve adjusters. At the readout the executive sponsor calls it a clear success: adjusters liked it, weekly usage grew, and no bad outcome was escalated. There is no written definition of success from before the pilot, and the adjusters' own pre-pilot triage accuracy was never measured. The sponsor wants to fund rollout to four hundred adjusters. What is the most defensible position to take?

options.A: Treat the pilot as producing no decision-grade evidence: agree now what result would have counted as failure, measure the adjusters' current baseline, and re-run against it.
options.B: Approve the rollout. Ten weeks of voluntary usage growth and positive adjuster sentiment are the leading indicators that matter for an assistive tool, and triage accuracy is hard to measure reliably at twelve-adjuster scale.
options.C: Approve the rollout and instrument an accuracy dashboard in production, where four hundred adjusters will generate a far larger sample than the pilot could and any quality problem will surface quickly.
options.D: Extend the pilot by a further ten weeks with more adjusters so the satisfaction and usage trends are confirmed on a bigger group before rollout budget is committed.

items.question: Why is an AI pilot that finished without success criteria agreed in advance treated as worthless evidence for a production go/no-go decision?

options.A: Pilots run on non-representative traffic almost by construction, so their measurements rarely generalise to production volumes or to the full diversity of real inputs.
options.B: Any outcome can be narrated as a success afterwards, so the pilot could not have disconfirmed the hypothesis it was meant to test.
options.C: Return on investment cannot be computed without a documented per-request cost, which pilots rarely capture.
options.D: Evaluation harnesses cannot be constructed retrospectively once the pilot traffic has already been served.
